standfirst: An uncle out of prison, a nephew with Asperger's, and a business that cleans the homes of people who died alone. Ten episodes, one death each, and it is not really a sad show so much as a generous one. These seven go to the same place, and the three at the bottom get recommended for the wrong reasons.

picks.why: The closest thing to a direct replacement that exists. A hospice team granting last wishes, a lead who does not want to be saved, and the same weekly structure of one stranger's life closed out with care. Both are loosely rooted in real practice. Difference: it is more conventionally plotted and its lead gets a redemption arc, where Geu-ru is never treated as a problem to be fixed.

The right answer for the register rather than the premise. Same interest in ordinary people carrying unbearable weight without announcing it, same restraint, same refusal to hand over catharsis on schedule. Difference: sixteen episodes and no case structure. It accumulates instead of resetting every hour.

Grim reapers whose actual job is preventing suicides, told case by case. It comes at the same subject from the opposite side: not what a death leaves behind in a room, but the hour before it. Difference: fantasy premise, sixteen episodes, and a much wider tonal range, including comedy that sits oddly next to this.

The other great autistic lead, and the light to Move to Heaven's dark. Episodic, warm, and equally careful not to write its protagonist as a lesson for anybody. Difference: it is a comfort show. Where Move to Heaven asks you to sit with a death every episode, Woo hands you a whale.

Two people at opposite ends of a life deciding to be responsible for each other, shot with the same still camera and the same interest in dignity over plot. Difference: no death of the week and no institutional anger. It is smaller and considerably kinder to you.

For the social-commentary half. Six episodes chasing military deserters, each one a portrait of somebody the system had already broken. Same method: one stranger per episode, no easy resolution offered. Difference: it is angry rather than tender, and the violence is explicit.

If you want the grief-of-the-week structure with the weight taken off. A pojangmacha where the owner settles other people's unfinished business, twelve episodes, found family, jokes. Difference: it is a fantasy comfort watch. Nobody is going to be destroyed, including you.

against.title: It's Okay to Not Be Okay
against.why: Suggested because it also features an autistic character and a mental-health frame. That character is a supporting brother, and the show belongs to a stylised, fairytale-gothic romance. Move to Heaven's whole method is documentary plainness.

against.title: Hospital Playlist
against.why: Both are gentle shows in which people die, and that is the entire overlap. Hospital Playlist is a hangout comedy that uses death as texture. Move to Heaven puts a stranger's entire life on the floor in front of you and asks you to look at it.

against.title: Racket Boys
against.why: The Tang Joon-sang pick, if he is the reason you are here. It is a warm rural sports comedy about teenagers. Genuinely good show, and it will not scratch this itch at all.
